content: Genital Chlamydia trachomatis infection during pregnancy can result in serious complications, including miscarriage, preterm labor, low birthweight, preterm rupture of membranes, increased perinatal mortality, postpartum endometritis, neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis, and pneumonia caused by C. trachomatis. This review aimed to identify the most effective and well-tolerated treatments for this infection to prevent maternal complications and adverse neonatal outcomes. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cluster-RCTs, but excluded quasi-randomized trials and cross-over designs. A total of 15 trials involving 1,754 pregnant women were included, with studies conducted in North America between 1982 and 2001. The quality of the studies varied, with only two trials having a low risk of bias across all domains. Four studies were excluded, and one trial is ongoing. Microbiological Cure (Primary Outcome) Antibiotics vs. Placebo: Erythromycin was associated with a higher likelihood of microbiological cure compared to placebo (average risk ratio [RR] 2.64, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.60 to 4.38; moderate-certainty evidence). Clindamycin also showed improved microbiological cure rates compared to placebo (RR 4.08, 95% CI 2.35 to 7.08; low-certainty evidence). However, in a small trial comparing amoxicillin to placebo, the results were unclear, with very low-certainty evidence (RR 2.00, 95% CI 0.59 to 6.79). One Antibiotic vs. Another Antibiotic: Amoxicillin showed little to no difference in microbiological cure rates compared to erythromycin (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.01; high-certainty evidence) or clindamycin (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.04; moderate-certainty evidence). When compared to azithromycin, the evidence was of very low certainty, and the effect was uncertain (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.12). Azithromycin and erythromycin likely have similar efficacy, though results slightly favored azithromycin (average RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.23; moderate-certainty evidence). Clindamycin and erythromycin also appeared to have similar efficacy (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.15; low-certainty evidence). Evidence was downgraded due to design limitations, inconsistency, and imprecision. Maternal Side Effects (Secondary Outcome) Antibiotics vs. Placebo: Side effects such as nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain were reported in two studies (495 women). However, there was no clear evidence that erythromycin caused more side effects than placebo, and a high level of heterogeneity was observed (average RR 2.93, 95% CI 0.36 to 23.76). In one small study comparing clindamycin to placebo, there was no clear difference in side effects (RR 6.35, 95% CI 0.38 to 107.45; 62 women). Reported side effects were mostly gastrointestinal and included resolving skin rashes. One Antibiotic vs. Another Antibiotic: When amoxicillin was compared to azithromycin, there was no clear difference in side effects (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.24 to 1.31; 36 women). However, amoxicillin was associated with fewer side effects compared to erythromycin (RR 0.31, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.46; 513 women). Side effects included nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramping, rash, and allergic reactions. Azithromycin (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.34; 374 women) and clindamycin (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.87; 183 women) were associated with fewer side effects compared to erythromycin. These side effects included nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal cramping. In one small study comparing amoxicillin to clindamycin, there was no clear difference in side effects (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.14 to 2.26; 107 women). Reported side effects included rash and gastrointestinal complaints. Other Secondary Outcomes Single trials reported on outcomes such as repeated infections, preterm birth, preterm rupture of membranes, perinatal mortality, and low birthweight. However, no clear differences were observed between treatments. Many secondary outcomes were not reported in the included studies. Authors' Conclusions Antibiotic treatment effectively achieves microbiological cure for C. trachomatis infection during pregnancy. There was no significant difference in efficacy between the antibiotics studied (amoxicillin, erythromycin, clindamycin, azithromycin) in terms of microbiological cure, repeated infections, or pregnancy complications (e.g., preterm birth, preterm rupture of membranes, low birthweight). However, azithromycin and clindamycin were associated with fewer side effects compared to erythromycin. The generalizability of these findings may be limited, as all studies were conducted in North America, and the study populations may differ in low-resource settings. Additionally, most trials were conducted in the 1990s and early 2000s, and patterns of antibiotic resistance may have changed since then. Further well-designed studies with larger sample sizes and conducted in diverse settings are needed to evaluate the most effective and well-tolerated treatments for C. trachomatis infection during pregnancy. Future studies should also report on the outcomes listed in this review.
